questions.question_text: After a $35\%$ increase, a swimming club has $918$ members. What percentage of the original does $918$ represent?

options.why: Subtracted the change from $100\%$, as if the membership had fallen.
Gave the size of the increase instead of what the new membership represents.
Treated the new membership as still equal to the original.

questions.question_text: After a $45\%$ decrease, a runner completes $22$ laps in a session. What percentage of the original does $22$ represent?

options.why: Added the change to $100\%$, as if the number of laps had risen.
Gave the size of the decrease instead of what the remaining laps represent.
Treated the reduced number of laps as still equal to the original.

questions.question_text: After a $7.5\%$ increase, a gym records $1290$ visits in a week. What percentage of the original does $1290$ represent?

options.why: Subtracted the change from $100\%$, as if visits had dropped.
Gave the size of the increase instead of what the new number of visits represents.
Treated the new number of visits as still equal to the original.

questions.question_text: A cyclist's weekly training distance increased by $60\%$. The increase was $27$ km. What percentage of the original does the $27$ km represent?

options.why: Read the $27$ km as the new distance rather than as the size of the increase.
Subtracted $60$ from $100$ instead of recognising the $27$ km as the change itself.
Treated the extra distance as the whole original training distance.

questions.solution_text:
'Increased by $27$ km' names the change, not the new distance.
$27$ km represents $60\%$ of the original.

Gave the size of the reduction instead of what the remaining players represent.
Treated the remaining players as still equal to the original field.
